source: Rolling Dynamics
Static friction makes rolling work: on a ramp a = g sin θ/(1 + I/(MR²)).
Students think static friction takes energy from an object rolling without slipping.

Rolling Without Slipping showed with energy that a hoop loses a race down a ramp to a solid ball. Newton's Second Law for Rotation lets us find the forces and the acceleration directly, and see what static friction is doing.

Take an object of mass $M$, radius $R$ and $I = cMR^2$ rolling down a ramp at angle $\theta$. Along the ramp: $$Mg\sin\theta - f = Ma.$$ About the center, only friction has a lever arm: $$fR = I\alpha = cMR^2\alpha.$$ Rolling without slipping links them: $a = R\alpha$. So $f = cMa$, and substituting, $Mg\sin\theta = Ma(1 + c)$.

$$a = \dfrac{g\sin\theta}{1 + I/(MR^2)}, \qquad f = \dfrac{I}{R^2}a.$$ Mass and radius cancel; only the shape factor $c = I/(MR^2)$ matters: solid ball 0.4, solid disk 0.5, hollow ball 0.67, hoop 1. Static friction must supply $f$, so rolling needs $\mu_s \ge \dfrac{c}{1 + c}\tan\theta$.
Hoop, solid disk, solid ball and hollow ball race down the same ramp. The smaller $I/(MR^2)$, the bigger the acceleration.
A solid ball rolls without slipping down a $30^\circ$ ramp. Find its acceleration and the least $\mu_s$ that allows rolling.
A ball on a ramp
$a = \dfrac{9.8\sin 30^\circ}{1 + 0.4} = \dfrac{4.9}{1.4} = 3.5\ \text{m/s}^2$ (sliding without friction it would be $4.9\ \text{m/s}^2$).
Friction needed: $f = 0.4Ma = 0.4(3.5)M = 1.4M$ (in newtons, with $M$ in kilograms).
$\mu_s \ge \dfrac{f}{Mg\cos\theta} = \dfrac{0.4}{1.4}\tan 30^\circ = 0.165$.
A hoop and a solid ball each roll from rest down a ramp, dropping $1.0\ \text{m}$. Find each one's speed at the bottom.
Speed at the bottom
Hoop $3.13\ \text{m/s}$; ball $3.74\ \text{m/s}$.
Energy: $Mgh = \tfrac{1}{2}Mv^2(1 + c)$, so $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2gh}{1 + c}}$.
Solid ball ($c = 0.4$): $v = \sqrt{19.6/1.4} = 3.74\ \text{m/s}$. The hoop puts half its energy into spinning; the ball only 2/7.

Why don't mass and radius matter? A bigger or heavier object of the same shape has more weight pulling it down the ramp, but proportionally more inertia, both for moving and for spinning. Only the shape, through $I/(MR^2)$, decides how the energy splits between moving and spinning.

Thinking static friction drains energy from a rolling object, so energy conservation fails. The contact point of a rolling object is momentarily at rest ($v_{\text{contact}} = v - R\omega = 0$), so friction acting there does no work. It moves energy from "moving" to "spinning" without losing any. Check: the energy method above, which ignores friction, gives the same answer as the force method, which includes it. (Kinetic friction during skidding is different; see From Skidding to Rolling.)
